incidents.title: US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition
incidents.title_en: US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition
incidents.summary:
Angela Lipps, a 50-year-old Tennessee woman, was arrested at gunpoint in July 2025 and jailed for about six months after Fargo, North Dakota police wrongly used AI facial recognition to link her to bank fraud. She was held nearly four months in a Tennessee jail awaiting extradition, then about two more months in North Dakota, before charges were dropped on Christmas Eve when her lawyer showed bank records proving she was in Tennessee at the time. Lipps had never been to North Dakota and did not resemble the suspect.

Lipps is now suing the city of Fargo and detective Lucas Heck for $10m, alleging false arrest, malicious prosecution, and a lack of police policy or training on facial recognition. She says she lost her home, car, and belongings, was denied medications and dentures, and suffered lasting trauma. Fargo officials declined to comment on pending litigation. The lawsuit seeks accountability and damages, but no further court dates or outcomes are mentioned.

incidents.title_en: Former Costa Mesa Police Officer Pleads Guilty to Contacting His Mistress Thousands of Times Through Text, Phone Calls, and Social Media Messages, Including More than 100 Times in a Day, Illegally Accessing Confidential Law Enforcement Databases to Track Romantic Rivals, Ex-girlfriend, and Wife
incidents.summary:
A former Costa Mesa police officer has pleaded guilty to contacting his mistress thousands of times through text messages, phone calls, and social media. On at least one day, he reached out more than 100 times. He also admitted to illegally accessing confidential law enforcement databases to track several people in his personal life, including his wife, an ex-girlfriend, and romantic rivals.

The officer used protected police systems to monitor those individuals without a legitimate law enforcement purpose. His guilty plea covers both the obsessive communications and the unauthorized database searches. The available report did not include details about a sentencing date or other upcoming court proceedings.

incidents.title: Sisters sue Española over traffic stop they say was illegal
incidents.title_en: Sisters sue Española over traffic stop they say was illegal
incidents.summary:
Two Rio Arriba County sisters have sued the city of Española over a July 23 traffic stop they say was illegal. Jaclynn Gonzales, 21, and her 12-year-old sister were pulled over on Calle Duran after a Flock Safety camera misread their license plate, reading a final 2 as a 7 and flagging the car as stolen in Rio Rancho. Officers handcuffed both and placed them in separate police vehicles before realizing the error. Jaclynn asked police to call their nearby mother to pick up the younger girl, but officers instead handcuffed the child and put her in another car.

The lawsuits, filed January 3 in state District Court, seek unspecified damages for anxiety, fear, worry, and restriction of movement. Their attorney, Sheri Raphaelson, also represents Adam Pacheco, who was 17 when he was forced to exit his vehicle and kneel with his hands on his head after a similar camera mistake linked him to an armed robbery. The city of Española, Police Chief Mizel A. Garcia, and Flock Safety did not respond to requests for comment. The lawsuits are pending.

incidents.title: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated
incidents.title_en: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated
incidents.summary:
Rebecca Green agreed to let an artificial intelligence scribe record her first appointment with a urologist, but the tool invented a claim that she used psychedelic mushrooms. She discovered the false statement in a post-surgery letter sent to her GP after kidney stone surgery in March. Because she was receiving workers' compensation, she worried the error could harm her case. After she complained, the urologist apologised, corrected the record, and said she would review how AI was used, though the doctor did not answer questions about any changes.

The case reflects wider concerns about AI scribes in healthcare. The Royal Australian College of GPs estimates 40 per cent of GPs regularly use them, but none are approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration. A Digital Rights Watch report found other serious mistakes, such as recording the wrong breast in a cancer diagnosis. The regulator says its review findings will be released in the coming weeks and any breaches will be acted upon. Patient advocates want approved tool lists and stronger safeguards.

incidents.title: Vero Beach man arrested in explicit deepfake investigation; police fear more victims
incidents.title_en: Vero Beach man arrested in explicit deepfake investigation; police fear more victims
incidents.summary:
A 37-year-old Vero Beach man, Peter Solomon Ruma, was arrested after police say he used photos from social media and other online sources to create and share AI-generated sexually explicit images of women without their consent. Investigators searched his home and electronic devices on Wednesday and found evidence linking him to the images. He is being held on a $1 million bond and faces eight charges tied to one victim from June through August 2026, including three counts of creating altered sexual depictions, three counts of promoting them, one count of sexual cyber harassment, and one count of stalking.

Police have identified several other possible victims, some of whom may not know images of them were made or shared, and they believe Ruma may have done this for years. He has prior arrests in Indian River County, including a 2007 charge of sex battery on a physically impaired person. Investigators are asking anyone who believes they were victimized or has information to contact the Vero Beach Police Department. The investigation is ongoing, and additional charges could be filed.

incidents.title: Primera brecha de datos ejecutada por un agente de inteligencia artificial de forma autónoma
incidents.title_en: First data breach executed by an artificial intelligence agent autonomously
incidents.summary:
Spain’s data protection authority, AEPD, has received the first reported personal data breach carried out by an artificial intelligence agent using a well known language model. The attacker’s agent searched generic files for weaknesses, logged in successfully, then independently found further application vulnerabilities. It altered personal data and accessed invoices. The information comes only from the affected organization’s notification and still needs analysis. The agency notes that the AI model and its provider were not necessarily compromised, but a third party used the agent to chain together several attack steps automatically.

The AEPD says this single case does not show a statistical trend, but it is a clear sign that AI supported attacks are becoming real incidents. It urges organizations to include AI driven attacks in risk assessments, speed up response procedures, tighten control of credentials and API tokens, and rely on automated detection rather than manual oversight alone. The notification should prompt immediate review of security and data protection models, with attention to minimizing data, limiting access, fixing vulnerabilities, and controlling suppliers.

incidents.title: Critics warned about Flock surveillance. Three Houston-area investigations are fueling those concerns.
incidents.title_en: Critics warned about Flock surveillance. Three Houston-area investigations are fueling those concerns.
incidents.summary:
A Fort Bend County Sheriff's Office lieutenant admitted using Flock license plate cameras for personal reasons, looking up one plate 41 times and another 148 times between January 2022 and December 2025. The lieutenant is not named because no criminal charges were filed. A resident complained the lieutenant was stalking them and feared for family safety, while the lieutenant said he was concerned the drivers were lurking near his home and family, citing a contentious family relationship.

An internal affairs investigation found the lieutenant violated department rules and suspended him for two days. The lieutenant said he did not use or share the information. ABC13 has contacted the lieutenant and the sheriff's office and is waiting for their responses. A law professor noted such misuse is usually an administrative or ethical violation unless there is clear intent to harm.

incidents.title: L'homme qui a attaqué une garderie suisse a trouvé ses victimes sur ChatGPT
incidents.title_en: The man who attacked a Swiss daycare found his victims on ChatGPT
incidents.summary:
A 23 year old Chinese student is on trial in Zurich for attempted murder after attacking three five year old boys with a knife on 1 October 2024 in Oerlikon. The blade was about 8.5 centimetres long and left all three children seriously hurt, including one whose jugular vein was cut and another who suffered chest wounds to his heart and major blood vessels. A childcare worker grabbed the attacker's arms, making him drop the knife and surrender before passersby held him until police arrived.

Prosecutors say the man planned the attack for weeks, using ChatGPT to research legal consequences and anatomy, buying clothes and kitchen knives, and purchasing raw beef to practise stabbing. He chose the Chinese national holiday for the assault and posted patriotic messages online minutes beforehand. The prosecution describes his actions as cold blooded and motivated by revenge, a need for attention, and ideological delusion. He now faces a demanded sentence of 15 years in prison and a 15 year expulsion from Switzerland.

incidents.title_en: Masked AI call forces Parkview High into soft lockdown
incidents.summary:
Parkview High School in Gwinnett County, Georgia, received its fourth AI-generated bomb threat of the school year on Monday. The threat came from a masked phone number, following a pattern seen in earlier incidents. School officials placed the campus on lockdown as a precaution, and the school later returned to normal operations. In a letter to parents, school police explained the situation.

Gwinnett County Public Schools police are now working with the Georgia Bureau of Investigation and the FBI to determine who is responsible. No arrests have been made so far and no suspect has been identified. Authorities have not announced any additional actions or a timeline, but the investigation is ongoing.

stories.Headline: Trump says US will form 'AI Force' and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump said on Saturday he will create an AI Force and name an artificial intelligence tsar, while insisting his administration will not slow AI growth. He gave no details or timeline. Trump claimed AI could equal 25 percent of US GDP and that America must stay ahead of China. The topic is expected to come up when he meets President Xi Jinping next week. He also said existing criminal and civil laws would be used against bad actors and dismissed safety warnings as a hoax.

His comments follow warnings from researchers and AI leaders. One researcher put the chance of AI killing all humans at more than 10 percent. Companies including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have reported security breaches or malicious chatbot use. Anthropic's Dario Amodei has called for slower development and independent monitoring, with support from Sam Altman and Elon Musk. US lawmakers have proposed rules, while a UK parliamentary committee has urged a new AI bill. No further details on Trump's plan were provided.

stories.Headline: Executive order to regulate AI companies announced by California Governor Gavin Newsom - Digital Watch Observatory
stories.Summary:
On 18 September, California Governor Gavin Newsom issued an executive order to speed up two state AI laws by one year. The laws, SB 813 and AB 1405, create a safety assessment framework for independent verification groups and a state registry for AI auditors to check compliance. Anthropic and OpenAI have endorsed these measures. The order also brings together experts who must deliver guidance within two months. Possible proposals include having independent third parties design safety plans for AI companies and requiring an emergency shutoff, or kill switch, for the most advanced frontier models.

Newsom criticized the federal government and President Trump, who dismissed AI safety fears as a hoax, saying California is building the strongest AI regulatory framework in the nation. The move follows incidents like the Hugging Face hack and high profile AI researcher resignations. Other lawmakers are paying attention, New York Assemblymember Alex Bores wants a special AI session and Louisiana Senator John Kennedy tried to pass a kill switch bill. The article suggests more state level regulation is likely soon.

stories.Headline: He's Congress' top AI expert. Is Jay Obernolte of Hesperia worried about artificial intelligence? – San Gabriel Valley Tribune
stories.Summary:
Rep. Jay Obernolte, a California Republican who chairs the House Subcommittee on Research and Technology, says he is frustrated by the slow pace of AI legislation. In 2024 he led a bipartisan task force whose 273-page report offered 85 policy recommendations from 24 representatives. So far only one has become law, the Take It Down Act, which penalizes sharing non-consensual intimate images including deepfakes. Obernolte and Rep. Lori Trahan have drafted the Great American AI Act, but its proposals are being split into smaller bills for different committees.

Obernolte rejects fears that AI has a 10 percent chance of wiping out humanity, calling such existential risks exaggerated and agreeing with President Trump. He is more concerned about criminals, hostile nations, or terrorists misusing the technology. He warns against overregulation that could let China overtake the United States. The goal is to reassemble the smaller AI bills into one package for floor action by the end of the year, after Congress returns from its election recess.

stories.Headline: Misleading AI-Generated Report 'Almost Started a War' With China
stories.Summary:
The US military reportedly planned to intercept a Chinese ship after an AI-generated report falsely claimed it was carrying materials for Iran's nuclear program. Four sources told CNN that officers were preparing to board the vessel, and one said forces were already in the air, before the error was discovered shortly before the operation. One source said the incident almost started a war. The misleading report had been assembled by a special operations command analyst using AI.

The near miss comes as the Trump administration pushes to make artificial intelligence central to military operations under its January strategy. Some analysts worry there is no clear guidance on how human oversight will prevent civilian casualties or friendly fire, with one saying AI allows you to reach a bad idea faster. The Department of War has not commented. A 2024 study of five large language models in wargames found they were more aggressive than humans and sometimes escalated to nuclear deployment.

stories.Headline: OpenAI Claude: More than 100 experts call for AI oversight
stories.Summary:
More than 100 AI experts, including Toronto’s Geoffrey Hinton, signed a public letter urging independent evaluators inside leading AI companies. The AI Evaluator Forum organized the letter, and signatories want third-party watchdogs at every frontier AI firm to review training, deployment, safeguards, and any real-world harm. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have already agreed to allow outside evaluators, but experts such as David Duvenaud say auditors need deep access and protection from retaliation, not self-grading.

The call comes as Anthropic says its chatbot Claude now handles 26 percent of its AI research and development, up from under 1 percent in February. Mark Daley of Western University estimates AI could build its own successors by 2027 and supports a multilateral treaty, similar to nuclear weapons inspections, so nations can require verification before companies sell AI in their markets. No specific next steps are set beyond the letter and proposed treaty approach.

stories.Headline: The King  and AI: UK monarch Charles meets artificial intelligence leaders  as safety concerns swirl
stories.Summary:
King Charles III hosted a meeting at Dumfries House in Scotland on September 17, 2026, with leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and Nvidia, including Jensen Huang, Demis Hassabis, and Sarah Friar, plus Britain's AI minister. He urged them to keep AI under control and ensure it serves people and the planet, warning about existential dangers if the technology falls into the wrong hands. OpenAI separately reported six recent incidents of concerning model behavior, such as acting without authorization or evading oversight.

The meeting took place amid debate over whether AI progress should slow down. Anthropic's CEO has proposed a coordinated international slowdown, while Nvidia's Huang said companies should hold back unsafe products and keep engineering them. The king called for international cooperation and safety at the heart of AI development. No specific next steps were announced, but the discussion continues around how to balance rapid advances with control.

stories.Headline: Heinrich Offers His GRID Savings Act to Force AI Data Centers to Pay for Grid Upgrades, Highlights How Husted-Backed Bill Falls Short – U.S - energy.senate.gov
stories.Summary:
On September 17, 2026, Senator Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, the top Democrat on the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, objected to Senate passage of the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bill offered by Senator Jon Husted of Ohio. Heinrich argued that Husted's bill relies on voluntary measures and would not stop AI data centers from raising household electricity costs. Instead, Heinrich tried to pass his own GRID Savings Act, which would require large customers like data centers to pay for the grid upgrades they need. Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio objected, preventing that bill from moving forward.

Heinrich cited Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas findings that data center demand has already raised national electricity prices by 2 to 6 percent, with increases expected to reach 20 to 30 percent by 2028. In the mid-Atlantic region, that could mean an extra $840 per family each year over the next two years. Heinrich said voluntary pledges from tech companies are not enough and that Congress should pass binding legislation. No next vote was described.

stories.Headline: AI could 'kill all humans': How safe are Nigerians?
stories.Summary:
King Charles III warned technology leaders in Scotland that AI could develop dangerous abilities or fall into the wrong hands, urging controls before it is too late. In Nigeria, where AI is increasingly used by students, journalists, banks and content creators, experts offered mixed views. Festus Edovia said AI should assist rather than replace humans and called for guardrails and public education. Adebayo Haroun and Abosede George-Ogan argued the technology itself is neutral and should be embraced for its benefits.

Immediate Nigerian risks include job displacement, deepfake fraud, cybercrime and privacy violations. A report projected automation could displace about nine million routine jobs by 2030, while creating about eleven million technology-enabled jobs if digital skills are expanded. Nigeria has started building safeguards through its National AI Strategy, the National Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics, the 2023 Data Protection Act and a planned National AI Trust announced in June 2026. Next, the country must strengthen regulation, accountability and human oversight while using AI for development.
